name: Lamplighters' Union
blurb: Every dusk, a man with a pole walked the streets of London lighting gas lamps one by one, and every dawn he walked them again to put them out. Electric lighting retired the trade by the 1930s. A handful of ceremonial lamplighters still walk London's parks.

name: Knocker-Uppers' Association
blurb: Before affordable alarm clocks, mill and dock workers in industrial Britain paid a knocker-upper a few pence a week to rap on their bedroom window with a long pole, or a pea shooter, until they woke. The trade survived in some northern towns into the 1970s.

name: Ice Harvesters' Guild
blurb: Crews sawed blocks of ice from frozen New England lakes each winter, packed them in sawdust, and shipped them as far as Calcutta. Frederic Tudor built an empire on it starting in 1806. Mechanical refrigeration melted the whole industry within a generation.

name: Human Computers' Society
blurb: For two centuries, 'computer' was a job title. Teams of people, very often women, worked long-hand through orbital mechanics, tide tables, and ballistics. In 1757 three of them predicted the return of Halley's comet. The electronic kind took over after 1945.

name: Switchboard Operators' Local
blurb: Every call once passed through a person who plugged a cord into the right jack by hand. The first exchange opened in New Haven in 1878. Direct dialing put most operators out of work by the 1960s, and the last manual exchanges closed in the 1980s.

name: Pinsetters' Brotherhood
blurb: Pin boys sat on a ledge at the end of the lane, dodging flying pins, resetting them by hand and rolling the ball back. It was fast, loud, and badly paid. The automatic pinsetter arrived in 1946 and cleared the ledge for good.

name: Rat Catchers' Fraternal Order
blurb: Victorian rat catchers worked with ferrets, terriers and bare hands, and the best of them sold live rats to sporting pubs on the side. Jack Black, self-styled rat catcher to Queen Victoria, wore a sash embroidered with rats. Modern pest control kept the job but lost the flair.

name: Town Criers' Guild
blurb: Before newspapers could reach a mostly illiterate public, the crier rang a bell and shouted the news: proclamations, market days, hangings. Harming a crier was harming the crown. Literacy and cheap print made the job a costume.

name: Telegraphists' Union
blurb: Telegraphists sent the world's messages by tapping dots and dashes at up to forty words a minute, and billed by the word, which is why telegrams sound the way they do. The telephone, then the fax, then everything else, shut the last commercial Morse circuits.

name: Lectors' Union
blurb: In Cuban and Floridian cigar factories, the workers pooled their wages to hire a lector who sat on a platform and read aloud all day: newspapers in the morning, Zola and Cervantes in the afternoon. Factory owners banned the tradition in 1931 for being too political. The radio finished it.
